problem: Classical probabilistic object search keeps an explicit belief over target locations but picks actions with handcrafted utility heuristics, while end-to-end deep RL learns adaptive policies but converges slowly and lacks uncertainty reasoning and interpretability.
motivation: Object search under partial observability and noisy detections needs both calibrated uncertainty modelling and adaptive long-horizon decisions. The paper observes that a Bayesian belief map is a compact, informative state that a learned policy can act on directly, instead of relying on a fixed utility function.
key_idea: Maintain a Dirichlet-based Bayesian belief map over object classes on the known occupancy grid, updated from calibrated YOLO detections, and train a DQN to choose cluster-centroid navigation goals from a belief/entropy/map tensor.
insight: Belief-based methods (BBUMS, BBDPS) beat non-belief baselines on success rate (Env.1: 0.87/1.00 vs PCSS 0.85; Env.2: 0.94/0.99 vs 0.89). Learning the goal choice pays off mainly in the larger map: BBDPS uses 109.10 actions vs 140.85 for BBUMS in Env.2 (~23% fewer). In the small Env.1 the handcrafted utility and the sweep are already efficient and BBDPS is less efficient (20.66 vs 13.00 actions), so the gain from learning grows with environment size.
method: Perception: YOLOv11 with the sigmoid head replaced by softmax and temperature-calibrated on MS COCO; detections are projected via depth and pose onto the occupancy grid and snapped to the nearest occupied cell.
Dirichlet belief map: each occupied cell holds a Dirichlet over K classes plus background, initialised uniform; posterior mean gives the class distribution.

Observation evidence: detection probabilities are rescaled to reserve 1/(K+1) mass for background; visible occupied cells with no detection give distance-decayed background evidence using the false-negative rate η.
Conservative Bayesian fusion: the Kaplan et al. update rule replaces the plain conjugate pseudo-count update to avoid overconfident posteriors under noisy detections.
Clustering abstraction: free cells are partitioned into k_ℓ clusters whose centroids are candidate goals; if all are visited without success the cluster count doubles (progressive refinement).

DQN over cluster centres: the input tensor has 4 channels (target posterior, normalised entropy, occupancy grid, robot position one-hot); it outputs a Q-map over free cells masked to admissible centroids, with ε-greedy selection; reward is -0.01 per primitive plus 1 on success.
Baselines built to isolate components: RWS (random walk), PCSS (greedy cluster sweep), BBUMS (belief with handcrafted utility using entropy, distance and target probability).

setting.backbone: DQN goal-selection policy over belief tensor (trained from scratch, one per environment) + YOLOv11 detector (softmax, temperature-calibrated)
setting.training_data: 5000 RL episodes per environment; 3 training target objects at fixed locations per environment, evaluated on a different held-out target; YOLO calibrated on MS COCO
setting.observation: RGB-D (1024x576, 90° HFOV) + known 2D occupancy grid (0.30 m) + robot pose
setting.action_space: high-level goals = cluster centroids on the grid, executed by shortest-path planning with move_forward / turn_left / turn_right primitives
setting.simulator: Habitat 3.0 (two indoor scenes: office and two-bedroom apartment)
setting.privileged: known occupancy grid map of the environment and robot pose (localization) given a priori

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 test episodes from distinct start poses, single held-out target (tv), horizon T=0.75N
numbers.extra: policy trained per environment; known occupancy grid; efficiency measured on 41 joint-success episodes
numbers.evidence: Table 1 Success rates across environments (Env. 1 BBDPS 1.00); Table 2 Efficiency over joint-success episodes (20.66 ± 4.23 actions, 4.05 ± 0.89 m)

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 test episodes from distinct start poses, single held-out target (laptop), horizon T=0.75N
numbers.extra: policy trained per environment; known occupancy grid; efficiency measured on 40 joint-success episodes

numbers_note: Custom two-scene Habitat 3.0 evaluation, not a standard benchmark. SR is printed as a fraction (0-1); it is kept as printed here. Efficiency numbers are means over joint-success episodes only.
results: BBDPS reaches SR 1.00 (Env.1) and 0.99 (Env.2), beating BBUMS (0.87/0.94), PCSS (0.85/0.89) and RWS (0.52/0.43). In the larger Env.2 it cuts actions by ~23% relative to BBUMS (109.10 vs 140.85) and distance by ~18%, but in Env.1 PCSS and BBUMS are more efficient.
limitations: Assumes a known occupancy grid and does not address joint mapping and semantic discovery; performance is bounded by detector quality.
The grid-based state requires a separate policy per environment, so there is no cross-scene generalisation.
Very small evaluation (two scenes, one held-out target each, 100 episodes), simulation only, with no comparison to published ObjectNav methods.
builds_on: Bayesian belief-based object search (Thrun probabilistic robotics)
Kaplan et al. conservative Dirichlet fusion
